Fireside chat at Sequoia Ascent 2026 from a ~week ago. Some highlights: The first theme I tried to push on is that LLMs are about a lot more than just speeding up what existed before (e.g. coding). Three examples of new horizons: 1. menugen: an app that can be fully engulfed by LLMs, with no classical code needed: input an image, output an image and an LLM can natively do the thing. 2. install .md skills instead of install .sh scripts. Why create a complex Software 1.0 bash script for e.g. installing a piece of software if you can write the installation out in words and say "just show this to your LLM". The LLM is an advanced interpreter of English and can intelligently target installation to your setup, debug everything inline, etc. 3. LLM knowledge bases as an example of something that was *impossible* with classical code because it's computation over unstructured data (knowledge) from arbitrary sources and in arbitrary formats, including simply text articles etc. I pushed on these because in every new paradigm change, the obvious things are always in the realm of speeding up or somehow improving what existed, but here we have examples of functionality that either suddenly perhaps shouldn't even exist (1,2), or was fundamentally not possible before (3). The second (ongoing) theme is trying to explain the pattern of jaggedness in LLMs. How it can be true that a single artifact will simultaneously 1) coherently refactor a 100,000-line code base *and* 2) tell you to walk to the car wash to wash your car. I previously wrote about the source of this as having to do with verifiability of a domain, here I expand on this as having to also do with economics because revenue/TAM dictates what the frontier labs choose to package into training data distributions during RL. You're either in the data distribution (on the rails of the RL circuits) and flying or you're off-roading in the jungle with a machete, in relative terms. Still not 100% satisfied with this, but it's an ongoing struggle to build an accurate model of LLM capabilities if you wish to practically take advantage of their power while avoiding their pitfalls, which brings me to... Last theme is the agent-native economy. The decomposition of products and services into sensors, actuators and logic (split up across all of 1.0/2.0/3.0 computing paradigms), how we can make information maximally legible to LLMs, some words on the quickly emerging agentic engineering and its skill set, related hiring practices, etc., possibly even hints/dreams of fully neural computing handling the vast majority of computation with some help from (classical) CPU coprocessors. self improvement prompt for codex Vaibhav (VB) Srivastav (@reach_vb) UPDATE: Came up with an even better version of this prompt after the feedback Ask Codex to look across your sessions, Memories, and Chronicle, identify patterns, reuse what already exists, and only create the smallest useful skill, subagent, or automation. "Look back over my recent work from the last 30 days, or all available history if shorter, and identify repeated manual workflows worth packaging. Use available evidence in this order: - Recent Codex sessions and task summaries. - Codex Memories and rollout summaries to find patterns repeated across sessions. - Chronicle, if enabled, to spot repeated work outside Codex. Use Chronicle for discovery only; confirm important details in the relevant source system when possible. - Existing skills, custom agents, and automations, so you reuse or extend what already exists instead of duplicating it. Look broadly for work that is repeated, time-consuming, error-prone, context-heavy, or benefits from a consistent process. Include workflows across coding, research, writing, planning, communication, operations, analysis, and personal administration. Only act on a candidate when it: - occurred at least twice, or is clearly likely to recur and costly to repeat; - has stable inputs, a repeatable procedure, and a clear output or stopping condition; - would materially improve speed, quality, consistency, or reliability; - is not already adequately covered. Choose the smallest appropriate form: - Skill: a reusable workflow or playbook. - Custom subagent: a bounded specialist role or investigation task suitable for delegation. - Automation: a scheduled or recurring check, report, reminder, or monitor. - Skip: work that is too one-off, ambiguous, sensitive, or poorly evidenced to package. First produce a compact shortlist with: - repeated workflow - supporting evidence and dates - frequency/confidence - recommended form: skill, subagent, automation, extend existing, or skip - why it is or is not worth creating Then create only the high-confidence missing items. Keep them narrow, practical, source-aware, and easy to validate. Do not create speculative, overlapping, or overly broad assets. Finish with: - what you created or extended - what you deliberately skipped - what needs more evidence before packaging" — https://nitter.net/reach_vb/status/2058538305872949490#m

Perplexity just open-sourced the tool they use internally to keep their own developers safe. 😨 It's called Bumblebee. It runs quietly on a developer's laptop and checks for any sneaky code, suspicious browser plugins, or AI tools that might be silently leaking access to your data. It covers Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, all of it. Here is why this matters now. For the last six months, hackers have been quietly slipping malicious code into the free building blocks that almost every app in the world is built on. When a developer installs one of these poisoned pieces, the attacker gets a backdoor into everything that developer touches. Including their AI tools and the keys that unlock them. Most security tools defend the finished product. Bumblebee defends the person building it. An independent security researcher read through the entire code and confirmed it is clean. No hidden tracking. No data collection. No backdoors. For two years, AI coding tools shipped with zero security defenses around them. Perplexity just shipped one. Free. Harvard University just voted to limit the number of A grades given in undergraduate classes to about 20% of the class. I’m not in favor of this. It deeply runs counter to how I believe education should be. We should hold a high bar, but also work mightily to support the success of 100% of learners, rather than a fraction. Harvard’s administration took this step — over the objections of a large fraction of the student body — to counter grade inflation. Grade inflation is real: Many universities have been awarding A and B grades to ever larger fractions of students, and this has caused grade point averages (GPAs) to become less useful as signals of student skill. At the same time, we want students to succeed. The heart of the question is the role of educational institutions. Should our goal be: - To help students succeed? - To judge students? Both of these have value. But my focus when working in education is almost entirely helping students succeed. To me, it is clear that many people want to learn, to be empowered, to build skills that let them do new things! This is what we focus on at DeepLearningAI. This philosophy is also why my online courses (going back to my early online Stanford courses on Coursera) permitted an unlimited number of retries for graded assignments. I believe in letting — and even encouraging — someone to redo something until they succeed. This is as opposed to standing in judgement of the fact they didn’t get it right the first time. Further, I want homework assignments to be designed primarily to help people practice and learn, rather than to judge their skill level. This is why I prefer to create “Practice Problems” and “Practice Labs” — questions that, when you think through them, help you to gain practice and reinforce what you know. As opposed to “Assessment Problems” designed primarily to judge skill. But won’t Harvard’s move make GPAs more meaningful and help prospective employers identify strong candidates? Having hired a large number of people from Harvard and other institutions, I can say confidently that GPA is not an important signal. We have screening and interviewing processes that give far more accurate ways to figure out if someone is truly skilled. I do not need a wider spread in applicant GPA scores to figure out who's really good! To be clear, there is also value in assessment. Even though standardized testing is much hated, high-quality tests like the SAT, ACT, GRE, TOEFL, etc. provide objective measures of ability in a domain. I find that most people want to learn and succeed. There are also people who want rigorous assessment (for example, to apply for school admissions), but this is a lesser need, and is not my focus when building educational products. Harvard is often described as an “elite” educational institution. There are two ways to be elite: One option involves limiting enrollments, and then even among admitted students, cap the number of people that do well at 20%. I would rather pursue a different path: Set a high bar and teach elite, cutting-edge skills, but strive relentlessly to help everyone succeed. This way, eliteness is defined not by excluding people but by helping as many people as possible to be excellent. [Original text: The Batch newsletter]

New course: Build AI agents that generate images and videos -- an under-explored frontier. A key to performance is having the agent evaluate its own output, and iterate to improve quality. This short course is built together with @googlecloudtech and taught by Katie Nguyen and Wafae Bakkali. You'll learn three evaluation techniques and combine them in an agent: image-text similarity scoring to check the output matches the prompt, an LLM judge that scores against custom criteria like brand consistency, and structured rubrics that break a prompt into verifiable yes/no questions like "is the subject in the frame?" and "does the camera motion match?" Skills you'll gain: - Learn image and video prompt engineering - Build an image agent that turns brand guidelines into UI mockups - Build a video agent that plans multi-scene explainers and animates reference frames with synchronized audio Join and build agents that create images and video! deeplearning.ai/courses/ai-a… Video

New course: Transformers in Practice. You'll get a practical view of how transformer-based LLMs work, so you can reason about their behavior, diagnose problems like slow inference, and make smarter decisions about deployment. This course is built in partnership with @AMD and taught by @realSharonZhou . You'll see how transformers generate text one token at a time, how the model decides which earlier words matter most when predicting the next one, and how techniques like quantization speed up inference on GPUs. This is not a video-only course; interactive visualizations throughout let you play with these concepts and build intuition that sticks. Skills you'll gain: - Understand why LLMs hallucinate, and RAG and chain-of-thought shape what they generate - Look inside the model to see how attention and layers combine to predict the next token - Diagnose inference bottlenecks and learn the techniques that speed up transformers on GPUs Join and understand what's really happening inside your LLMs: deeplearning.ai/courses/tran… Video

There will be no AI jobpocalypse. The story that AI will lead to massive unemployment is stoking unnecessary fear. AI — like any other technology — does affect jobs, but telling overblown stories of large-scale unemployment is irresponsible and damaging. Let’s put a stop to it. I’ve expressed skepticism about the jobpocalypse in previous posts. I’m glad to see that the popular press is now pushing back on this narrative. The image below features some recent headlines. Software engineering is the sector most affected by AI tools, as coding agents race ahead. Yet hiring of software engineers remains strong! So while there are examples of AI taking away jobs, the trends strongly suggest the net job creation is vastly greater than the job destruction — just like earlier waves of technology. Further, despite all the exciting progress in AI, the U.S. unemployment rate remains a healthy 4.3%. Why is the AI jobpocalypse narrative so popular? For one thing, frontier AI labs have a strong incentive to tell stories that make AI technology sound more powerful. At their most extreme, they promote science-fiction scenarios of AI “taking over” and causing human extinction. If a technology can replace many employees, surely that technology must be very valuable! Also, a lot of SaaS software companies charge around $100-$1000 per user/year. But if an AI company can replace an employee who makes $100,000 — or make them 50% more productive — then charging even $10,000 starts to look reasonable. By anchoring not to typical SaaS prices but to salaries of employees, AI companies can charge a lot more. Additionally, businesses have a strong incentive to talk about layoffs as if they were caused by AI. After all, talking about how they’re using AI to be far more productive with fewer staff makes them look smart. This is a better message than admitting they overhired during the pandemic when capital was abundant due to low interest rates and a massive government financial stimulus. To be clear, I recognize that AI is causing a lot of people’s work to change. This is hard. This is stressful. (And to some, it can be fun.) I empathize with everyone affected. At the same time, this is very different from predicting a collapse of the job market. Societies are capable of telling themselves stories for years that have little basis in reality and lead to poor society-wide decision making. For example, fears over nuclear plant safety led to under-investment in nuclear power. Fears of the “population bomb” in the 1960s led countries to implement harsh policies to reduce their populations. And worries about dietary fat led governments to promote unhealthy high-sugar diets for decades. Now that mainstream media is openly skeptical about the jobpocalypse, I hope these stories will start to lose their teeth (much like fears of AI-driven human extinction have). Contrary to the predictions of an AI jobpocalypse, I predict the opposite: There will be an AI jobapalooza! AI will lead to a lot more good AI engineering jobs, and I’m also optimistic about the future of the overall job market. What AI engineers do will be different from traditional software engineering, and many of these jobs will be in businesses other than traditional large employers of developers. In non-AI roles, too, the skills needed will change because of AI. That makes this a good time to encourage more people to become proficient in AI, and make sure they’re ready for the different but plentiful jobs of the future! Researchers cracked the hidden order behind how AI learns. Loss curves tell you a model is improving. They don't say which skills form, or in what order. A new paper proposes the Implicit Curriculum Hypothesis. Pretraining follows a hidden, predictable order across families. Researchers built 91 tasks covering string operations, morphology, translation, logic, and math. They tracked 9 open-weight models from 410M to 13B parameters. The sequence was strikingly consistent across runs: > Simple copying emerges first > Then morphology and translation appear > Basic arithmetic follows after that > Complex reasoning shows up last Composite skills almost always emerge after their components. Spearman correlation hit .81 across 45 model pairs. The structure also lives inside the network. Tasks with similar internal representations follow similar learning curves. They predicted held-out trajectories with R² up to .84, without running evaluations. So how early could you spot a frontier run drifting?

highlights.text_original: This works really well btw, at the end of your query ask your LLM to "structure your response as HTML", then view the generated file in your browser. I've also had some success asking the LLM to present its output as slideshows, etc. More generally, imo audio is the human-preferred input to AIs but vision (images/animations/video) is the preferred output from them. Around a ~third of our brains are a massively parallel processor dedicated to vision, it is the 10-lane superhighway of information into brain. As AI improves, I think we'll see a progression that takes advantage: 1) raw text (hard/effortful to read) 2) markdown (bold, italic, headings, tables, a bit easier on the eyes) <-- current default 3) HTML (still procedural with underlying code, but a lot more flexibility on the graphics, layout, even interactivity) <-- early but forming new good default ...4,5,6,... n) interactive neural videos/simulations Imo the extrapolation (though the technology doesn't exist just yet) ends in some kind of interactive videos generated directly by a diffusion neural net. Many open questions as to how exact/procedural "Software 1.0" artifacts (e.g. interactive simulations) may be woven together with neural artifacts (diffusion grids), but generally something in the direction of the recently viral nitter.net/zan2434/status/2046982… There are also improvements necessary and pending at the input. Audio nor text nor video alone are not enough, e.g. I feel a need to point/gesture to things on the screen, similar to all the things you would do with a person physically next to you and your computer screen. TLDR The input/output mind meld between humans and AIs is ongoing and there is a lot of work to do and significant progress to be made, way before jumping all the way into neuralink-esque BCIs and all that. actu.text_fr: MiniMax, un modèle et agent open source de premier plan, est maintenant alimenté par l'infrastructure de recherche de Perplexity. MiniMax Agent utilise désormais la recherche @perplexity_ai. Nous avons comparé 3 fournisseurs de recherche AI-native sur plus de 700 tâches d'agents. Perplexity a fourni la meilleure combinaison de qualité de réponse et de densité d'extraits : plus de preuves utiles par token, moins de contexte non pertinent, et un coût de bout en bout plus faible. Comparé à Serper, notre précédent défaut : Appels d'outils par tâche : 17,8 contre 32,6 (réduction de 45%) Utilisation de tokens : 94,6M contre 162,3M (réduction de 42%) Taux de réussite : augmentation de 2% Coût total : 27% de réduction des économies totales Dans les flux de travail d'agents, la recherche n'est pas une recherche unique. C'est une boucle. De meilleurs extraits signifient un meilleur ancrage. Un meilleur ancrage signifie moins de recherches, moins de contexte, de meilleures réponses et un coût inférieur. Une bonne recherche peut économiser 14 mauvaises. Maintenant disponible dans MiniMax Agent.
actu.text_original: MiniMax, a leading open source model and agent, is now powered by Perplexity’s search infrastructure MiniMax_Agent (@MiniMaxAgent) MiniMax Agent now uses @perplexity_ai Search. We benchmarked 3 AI-native search providers across 700+ agent tasks. Perplexity delivered the best combination of answer quality and snippet density: more useful evidence per token, less irrelevant context, and lower end-to-end cost. Compared with Serper, our previous default: ⚡Tool calls per task: 17.8 vs 32.6 (45% reduction) 💰Token usage: 94.6M vs. 162.3M (42% reduction) 🔍Pass rate: +2% increase Total cost: 27% decrease in total cost savings In agent workflows, search is not a one-shot lookup. It is a loop. Better snippets mean better grounding. Better grounding means fewer searches, less context, better answers, and lower cost. One good search can save 14 bad ones. Now shipping in MiniMax Agent. agent.minimax.io/ — https://nitter.net/MiniMaxAgent/status/2057844100205031779#m

Nous l'avons découvert dans une quête secondaire pour pousser notre modèle sur les problèmes les plus difficiles. Pendant près de 80 ans, les mathématiciens ont cru que les meilleures solutions possibles ressemblaient à des grilles carrées. actu.text_fr: Très fier qu'un modèle OpenAI ait réfuté la conjecture de la distance unitaire d'Erdős depuis longtemps, avec une preuve élégante et complexe qui applique des idées sophistiquées de la théorie des nombres algébriques à la géométrie. Pour quelque raison que ce soit, les mathématiques ont été le domaine le plus propice aux percées de recherche avec l'IA. Je considère que c'est une chance que ce soit finalement les mathématiques - un domaine où les experts ont été disposés à s'engager profondément avec nous, et avec les preuves générées par nos modèles. J'en suis reconnaissant, et je ne le prends pas pour acquis. Les mathématiques sont une entreprise artistique, et peut-être que pour les artistes, c'est précisément leur appréciation de l'art qui les sauve du sentiment potentiellement grotesque d'une machine en produisant. Notre objectif n'est pas de remplacer les humains. Nous visons à tracer une voie où les humains continuent de jouer un rôle important, même en construisant une IA exceptionnellement puissante. Je suis enthousiaste à l'idée d'utiliser les mathématiques comme domaine pour explorer ces voies, et @SebastienBubeck , @merettm , et moi sommes impatients de collaborer avec la communauté mathématique élargie pour les tracer ensemble. N'hésitez pas à nous contacter si vous êtes intéressé ! Je suis optimiste quant au fait que cela nous aidera à naviguer dans l'impact de l'IA sur la société dans des domaines comme le codage et la collaboration générale.

Math is an artistic endeavor, and perhaps for artists, it is precisely their appreciation for art that saves them from the possibly grotesque feeling of a machine producing it. Our goal is not to replace humans. We aim to chart a path forward where humans continue to have a significant role to play, even as we build exceptionally powerful AI. I am excited to use math as a domain to explore these paths, and @SebastienBubeck , @merettm , and I are excited to engage with the broader mathematical community to chart them together. actu.text_fr: Meta prévoit d'alimenter ses centres de données IA avec de l'énergie solaire transmise depuis l'espace. Si cela fonctionne, les fermes solaires pourraient produire de l'énergie 24h/24 et 7j/7 sans batteries ni générateurs de secours. L'entreprise derrière tout cela est Overview Energy - elle veut lancer 1000 satellites en orbite, à 35 000 km au-dessus de l'équateur, où la lumière du soleil est constante. Pour contexte, les centres de données de Meta ont utilisé plus de 18 000 gigawattheures d'électricité l'année dernière. Assez pour alimenter 1,7 million de foyers américains pendant un an. Chaque satellite collecte l'énergie solaire, la convertit en un large faisceau de lumière proche infrarouge, et le dirige vers des fermes solaires existantes au sol. Les fermes convertissent la lumière en électricité, comme elles le font avec la lumière du soleil. Contrairement aux lasers haute puissance ou aux faisceaux micro-ondes, cette lumière infrarouge est suffisamment sûre pour être regardée directement. Les fermes solaires sont normalement inactives la nuit, donc ce système résout ce problème... depuis l'espace. Technologie vraiment fascinante. Vidéo
actu.text_original: Meta is planning to power its AI data centers with solar energy beamed from space. If it works, solar farms could produce power 24/7 without batteries or backup generators. The company behind it all is Overview Energy -- they want to launch 1,000 satellites into orbit, 22,000 miles above the equator, where sunlight is constant. For context, Meta's data centers used over 18,000 gigawatt-hours of electricity last year. Enough to power 1.7 million American homes for a year. Each satellite collects solar energy, converts it into a wide beam of near-infrared light, and aims it at existing solar farms on the ground. The farms convert the light into electricity, just like they do with sunlight. Unlike high-power lasers or microwave beams, this infrared light is safe enough to stare directly into. Solar farms normally sit idle at night, so this system fixes that... from space. Really fascinating tech. Video

actu.text_fr: Les chercheurs ont déchiffré l'ordre caché derrière la façon dont l'IA apprend. Les courbes de perte vous indiquent qu'un modèle s'améliore. Elles ne disent pas quelles compétences se forment, ni dans quel ordre. Un nouveau papier propose l'Hypothèse du Curriculum Implicite. Le pré-entraînement suit un ordre caché et prévisible à travers les familles. Les chercheurs ont construit 91 tâches couvrant les opérations sur chaînes de caractères, la morphologie, la traduction, la logique et les mathématiques. Ils ont suivi 9 modèles open-weight de 410M à 13B paramètres. La séquence était remarquablement cohérente entre les exécutions : > La copie simple émerge en premier > Ensuite, la morphologie et la traduction apparaissent > L'arithmétique de base suit après > Le raisonnement complexe apparaît en dernier Les compétences composites émergent presque toujours après leurs composants. La corrélation de Spearman a atteint 0,81 sur 45 paires de modèles. La structure vit également à l'intérieur du réseau. Les tâches avec des représentations internes similaires suivent des courbes d'apprentissage similaires. Ils ont prédit des trajectoires réservées avec un R² allant jusqu'à 0,84, sans exécuter d'évaluations. Alors, quand pourrait-on repérer une exécution de pointe qui dérive ?
actu.text_original: Researchers cracked the hidden order behind how AI learns. Loss curves tell you a model is improving. They don't say which skills form, or in what order. A new paper proposes the Implicit Curriculum Hypothesis. Pretraining follows a hidden, predictable order across families. Researchers built 91 tasks covering string operations, morphology, translation, logic, and math. They tracked 9 open-weight models from 410M to 13B parameters. The sequence was strikingly consistent across runs: > Simple copying emerges first > Then morphology and translation appear > Basic arithmetic follows after that > Complex reasoning shows up last Composite skills almost always emerge after their components. Spearman correlation hit .81 across 45 model pairs. The structure also lives inside the network. Tasks with similar internal representations follow similar learning curves. They predicted held-out trajectories with R² up to .84, without running evaluations. So how early could you spot a frontier run drifting?

actu.text_fr: Fireside chat chez Sequoia Ascent 2026 d'il y a environ une semaine. Quelques points forts : Le premier thème que j'ai essayé de promouvoir est que les LLM sont bien plus que de simples accélérateurs de ce qui existait auparavant (par exemple, le codage). Trois exemples de nouveaux horizons : 1. menugen : une application qui peut être entièrement engloutie par les LLM, sans code classique nécessaire : entrer une image, sortir une image et un LLM peut nativement faire la chose. 2. installer .md compétences au lieu d'installer des scripts .sh. Pourquoi créer un script bash complexe de Software 1.0 pour, par exemple, installer un logiciel si vous pouvez décrire l'installation en mots et dire "montrez simplement ceci à votre LLM". Le LLM est un interpréteur avancé de l'anglais et peut cibler intelligemment l'installation sur votre configuration, déboguer tout en ligne, etc. 3. Les bases de connaissances LLM comme exemple de quelque chose qui était *impossible* avec le code classique car il s'agit de calcul sur des données non structurées (connaissances) provenant de sources arbitraires et dans des formats arbitraires, y compris simplement des articles textuels, etc. J'ai insisté sur ces points car dans chaque changement de paradigme, les choses évidentes sont toujours dans le domaine de l'accélération ou de l'amélioration d'une manière ou d'une autre de ce qui existait, mais ici nous avons des exemples de fonctionnalités qui soit devraient soudainement peut-être même pas exister (1,2), soit étaient fondamentalement impossibles auparavant (3). Le deuxième thème (en cours) est d'essayer d'expliquer le schéma de "jaggedness" dans les LLM. Comment il peut être vrai qu'un seul artefact réécrive de manière cohérente une base de code de 100 000 lignes *et* vous dise d'aller à la station-service pour laver votre voiture. J'ai précédemment écrit sur la source de cela comme ayant à voir avec la vérifiabilité d'un domaine, ici je l'étends comme ayant aussi à voir avec l'économie car les revenus/TAM dictent ce que les laboratoires de pointe choisissent d'empaqueter dans les distributions de données d'entraînement pendant le RL. Soit vous êtes dans la distribution de données (sur les rails des circuits RL) et vous volez, soit vous êtes hors route dans la jungle avec une machette, en termes relatifs. Toujours pas 100% satisfait de cela, mais c'est une lutte continue pour construire un modèle précis des capacités des LLM si vous souhaitez profiter pratiquement de leur puissance tout en évitant leurs piètoires, ce qui m'amène à... Le dernier thème est l'économie native des agents. La décomposition des produits et services en capteurs, actionneurs et logique (répartis sur tous les paradigmes informatiques 1.0/2.0/3.0), comment nous pouvons rendre l'information maximalement lisible par les LLM, quelques mots sur l'ingénierie agentique rapidement émergente et son ensemble de compétences, les pratiques d'embauche associées, etc., voire même des indices/rêves de calcul entièrement neural gérant la grande majorité des calculs avec un peu d'aide des coprocesseurs (CPU) (classiques). Stephanie Zhan (@stephzhan) @karpathy et moi sommes de retour ! Chez @sequoia AI Ascent 2026. Et beaucoup de choses ont changé. L'année dernière, il a inventé le "vibe coding". Cette année, il se sent plus à la traîne que jamais en tant que programmeur. Le grand changement : le "vibe coding" a élevé le niveau de base. L'ingénierie agentique élève le plafond. Nous parlons de ce que signifie construire sérieusement à l'ère des agents. Pas seulement aller plus vite. actu.text_original: Fireside chat at Sequoia Ascent 2026 from a ~week ago. Some highlights: The first theme I tried to push on is that LLMs are about a lot more than just speeding up what existed before (e.g. coding). Three examples of new horizons: 1. menugen: an app that can be fully engulfed by LLMs, with no classical code needed: input an image, output an image and an LLM can natively do the thing. 2. install .md skills instead of install .sh scripts. Why create a complex Software 1.0 bash script for e.g. installing a piece of software if you can write the installation out in words and say "just show this to your LLM". The LLM is an advanced interpreter of English and can intelligently target installation to your setup, debug everything inline, etc. 3. LLM knowledge bases as an example of something that was *impossible* with classical code because it's computation over unstructured data (knowledge) from arbitrary sources and in arbitrary formats, including simply text articles etc. I pushed on these because in every new paradigm change, the obvious things are always in the realm of speeding up or somehow improving what existed, but here we have examples of functionality that either suddenly perhaps shouldn't even exist (1,2), or was fundamentally not possible before (3). The second (ongoing) theme is trying to explain the pattern of jaggedness in LLMs. How it can be true that a single artifact will simultaneously 1) coherently refactor a 100,000-line code base *and* 2) tell you to walk to the car wash to wash your car. I previously wrote about the source of this as having to do with verifiability of a domain, here I expand on this as having to also do with economics because revenue/TAM dictates what the frontier labs choose to package into training data distributions during RL. You're either in the data distribution (on the rails of the RL circuits) and flying or you're off-roading in the jungle with a machete, in relative terms. Still not 100% satisfied with this, but it's an ongoing struggle to build an accurate model of LLM capabilities if you wish to practically take advantage of their power while avoiding their pitfalls, which brings me to... Last theme is the agent-native economy. The decomposition of products and services into sensors, actuators and logic (split up across all of 1.0/2.0/3.0 computing paradigms), how we can make information maximally legible to LLMs, some words on the quickly emerging agentic engineering and its skill set, related hiring practices, etc., possibly even hints/dreams of fully neural computing handling the vast majority of computation with some help from (classical) CPU coprocessors. Stephanie Zhan (@stephzhan) @karpathy and I are back! At @sequoia AI Ascent 2026. And a lot has changed. Last year, he coined “vibe coding”. This year, he’s never felt more behind as a programmer. The big shift: vibe coding raised the floor. Agentic engineering raises the ceiling. We talk about what it means to build seriously in the agent era. Not just moving faster. Building new things, with new tools, while preserving the parts that still require human taste, judgment, and understanding. Video — https://nitter.net/stephzhan/status/2049518659513852109#m

Tout dépend de votre idée branchée sur le zeitgeist culturel, puis de votre style d'exécution qui est basé sur qui vous êtes en tant que personne. Chaque petit détail que vous expérimentez influence les choix que vous faites lors de la construction d'un produit. De petits détails infimes que vous faites différemment et qui sont incommensurables mais qui s'avèrent être une grande raison pour laquelle les utilisateurs aiment votre produit plutôt que d'autres. Pour moi, le moyen le plus simple d'acquérir plus d'expérience de vie a toujours été de voyager, encore mieux voyager pendant de très longues périodes, vivre dans des endroits étrangers par vous-même pendant des mois (peut-être des années), de préférence en solo, quelque chose vous arrive qui vous change en tant que personne. Vous voulez faire cela dans votre 20s/30s mais vous pouvez le faire à tout âge, c'est juste que si vous n'êtes plus célibataire, votre style de voyage change généralement en motifs plus normaux mais vous pouvez toujours le faire. Allez dans des endroits où peu d'autres personnes vont, je parle toujours de la Chine parce que très peu de gens la visitent, et pourtant c'est un leader mondial maintenant dans tant de choses, vous apprendrez tant de choses juste en y étant. tips.text_fr:
Astuce pour Codex : demandez-lui de regarder dans vos sessions, vos souvenirs et votre historique, d'identifier les motifs, de réutiliser ce qui existe déjà, et de créer uniquement la compétence, le sous-agent ou l'automatisation la plus petite et utile.

"Regarde mon travail récent des 30 derniers jours, ou tout l'historique disponible s'il est plus court, et identifie les flux de travail manuels répétés qui méritent d'être packagés. Utilise les preuves disponibles dans cet ordre :
- Sessions Codex récentes et résumés de tâches.
- Souvenirs Codex et résumés de déploiement pour trouver des motifs répétés entre les sessions.
- Chronicle, s'il est activé, pour repérer le travail répété en dehors de Codex. Utilise Chronicle pour la découverte uniquement ; confirme les détails importants dans le système source pertinent lorsque c'est possible.
- Compétences, agents personnalisés et automatisations existants, afin de réutiliser ou d'étendre ce qui existe déjà au lieu de le dupliquer.
Recherche largement les travaux qui sont répétés, chronophages, sujets aux erreurs, lourds en contexte, ou qui bénéficient d'un processus cohérent.
N'agis sur un candidat que s'il :
- s'est produit au moins deux fois, ou est clairement susceptible de réapparaître et coûteux à répéter ;
- a des entrées stables, une procédure répétable, et une sortie claire ou une condition d'arrêt ;
- améliorerait matériellement la vitesse, la qualité, la cohérence ou la fiabilité ;
- n'est pas déjà adéquatement couvert.
Choisis la forme la plus petite appropriée :
- Compétence : un flux de travail ou un playbook réutilisable.
- Agent personnalisé : un rôle de spécialiste délimité ou une tâche d'investigation adaptée à la délégation.
- Automatisation : une vérification, un rapport, un rappel ou un moniteur programmé ou récurrent.
- Ignorer : travail trop ponctuel, ambigu, sensible ou mal étayé pour être packagé.
Produis d'abord une liste compacte avec :
- flux de travail répété
- preuves et dates de support
- fréquence/confiance
- forme recommandée : compétence, sous-agent, automatisation, extension existante, ou ignorer
- pourquoi il vaut la peine ou non de le créer
Puis crée uniquement les éléments à haute confiance.
Garde-les ciblés, pratiques, conscients de la source et faciles à valider.
Ne crée pas d'éléments spéculatifs, qui se chevauchent ou trop larges.
Termine avec :
- ce que tu as créé ou étendu
- ce que tu as délibérément ignoré
- ce qui nécessite plus de preuves avant d'être packagé"
tips.text_original:
self improvement prompt for codex Vaibhav (VB) Srivastav (@reach_vb) UPDATE: Came up with an even better version of this prompt after the feedback Ask Codex to look across your sessions, Memories, and Chronicle, identify patterns, reuse what already exists, and only create the smallest useful skill, subagent, or automation. "Look back over my recent work from the last 30 days, or all available history if shorter, and identify repeated manual workflows worth packaging. Use available evidence in this order:
- Recent Codex sessions and task summaries.
- Codex Memories and rollout summaries to find patterns repeated across sessions.
- Chronicle, if enabled, to spot repeated work outside Codex. Use Chronicle for discovery only; confirm important details in the relevant source system when possible.
- Existing skills, custom agents, and automations, so you reuse or extend what already exists instead of duplicating it.
Look broadly for work that is repeated, time-consuming, error-prone, context-heavy, or benefits from a consistent process. Only act on a candidate when it:
- occurred at least twice, or is clearly likely to recur and costly to repeat;
- has stable inputs, a repeatable procedure, and a clear output or stopping condition;
- would materially improve speed, quality, consistency, or reliability;
- is not already adequately covered. Choose the smallest appropriate form:
- Skill: a reusable workflow or playbook.
- Custom subagent: a bounded specialist role or investigation task suitable for delegation.
- Automation: a scheduled or recurring check, report, reminder, or monitor.
- Skip: work that is too one-off, ambiguous, sensitive, or poorly evidenced to package. First produce a compact shortlist with:
- repeated workflow
- supporting evidence and dates
- frequency/confidence
- recommended form: skill, subagent, automation, extend existing, or skip
- why it is or is not worth creating Then create only the high-confidence missing items. Keep them narrow, practical, source-aware, and easy to validate. Do not create speculative, overlapping, or overly broad assets. Finish with:
- what you created or extended
- what you deliberately skipped
- what needs more evidence before packaging"

idees.text_original: Harvard University just voted to limit the number of A grades given in undergraduate classes to about 20% of the class. I’m not in favor of this. It deeply runs counter to how I believe education should be. We should hold a high bar, but also work mightily to support the success of 100% of learners, rather than a fraction. Harvard’s administration took this step — over the objections of a large fraction of the student body — to counter grade inflation. Grade inflation is real: Many universities have been awarding A and B grades to ever larger fractions of students, and this has caused grade point averages (GPAs) to become less useful as signals of student skill. At the same time, we want students to succeed. The heart of the question is the role of educational institutions. Should our goal be: - To help students succeed? - To judge students? Both of these have value. But my focus when working in education is almost entirely helping students succeed. To me, it is clear that many people want to learn, to be empowered, to build skills that let them do new things! This is what we focus on at DeepLearningAI. This philosophy is also why my online courses (going back to my early online Stanford courses on Coursera) permitted an unlimited number of retries for graded assignments. I believe in letting — and even encouraging — someone to redo something until they succeed. This is as opposed to standing in judgement of the fact they didn’t get it right the first time. Further, I want homework assignments to be designed primarily to help people practice and learn, rather than to judge their skill level. This is why I prefer to create “Practice Problems” and “Practice Labs” — questions that, when you think through them, help you to gain practice and reinforce what you know. As opposed to “Assessment Problems” designed primarily to judge skill. But won’t Harvard’s move make GPAs more meaningful and help prospective employers identify strong candidates? Having hired a large number of people from Harvard and other institutions, I can say confidently that GPA is not an important signal. We have screening and interviewing processes that give far more accurate ways to figure out if someone is truly skilled. I do not need a wider spread in applicant GPA scores to figure out who's really good! To be clear, there is also value in assessment. Even though standardized testing is much hated, high-quality tests like the SAT, ACT, GRE, TOEFL, etc. provide objective measures of ability in a domain. I find that most people want to learn and succeed. There are also people who want rigorous assessment (for example, to apply for school admissions), but this is a lesser need, and is not my focus when building educational products. Harvard is often described as an “elite” educational institution. There are two ways to be elite: One option involves limiting enrollments, and then even among admitted students, cap the number of people that do well at 20%. I would rather pursue a different path: Set a high bar and teach elite, cutting-edge skills, but strive relentlessly to help everyone succeed. This way, eliteness is defined not by excluding people but by helping as many people as possible to be excellent. [Original text: The Batch newsletter]

idees.text_fr: Il n'y aura pas de "jobpocalypse" de l'IA. L'histoire selon laquelle l'IA entraînera un chômage massif attise des craintes inutiles. L'IA - comme toute autre technologie - affecte les emplois, mais raconter des histoires exagérées de chômage à grande échelle est irresponsable et préjudiciable. Mettons-y fin. J'ai exprimé mon scepticisme quant à la "jobpocalypse" dans des posts précédents. Je suis heureux de voir que la presse populaire s'oppose maintenant à ce narratif. L'image ci-dessous présente quelques gros titres récents. L'ingénierie logicielle est le secteur le plus touché par les outils d'IA, alors que les agents de codage progressent rapidement. Pourtant, le recrutement d'ingénieurs logiciels reste fort ! Donc, bien qu'il existe des exemples d'IA prenant des emplois, les tendances suggèrent fortement que la création nette d'emplois est largement supérieure à la destruction d'emplois - tout comme lors des vagues technologiques précédentes. De plus, malgré tous les progrès passionnants de l'IA, le taux de chômage américain reste sain à 4,3%. Pourquoi le narratif de la "jobpocalypse" de l'IA est-il si populaire ? D'une part, les laboratoires d'IA de pointe ont un fort intérêt à raconter des histoires qui rendent la technologie IA plus puissante. À leur extrême, ils promeuvent des scénarios de science-fiction où l'IA "prend le contrôle" et provoque l'extinction humaine. Si une technologie peut remplacer de nombreux employés, alors cette technologie doit être très précieuse ! De plus, beaucoup d'entreprises SaaS facturent environ 100 à 1000 $ par utilisateur/an. Mais si une entreprise d'IA peut remplacer un employé qui gagne 100 000 $ - ou le rendre 50% plus productif - alors facturer même 10 000 $ commence à sembler raisonnable. En s'ancrant non pas aux prix SaaS typiques, mais aux salaires des employés, les entreprises d'IA peuvent facturer beaucoup plus. De plus, les entreprises ont un fort intérêt à parler des licenciements comme s'ils étaient causés par l'IA. Après tout, parler de la façon dont elles utilisent l'IA pour être beaucoup plus productives avec moins de personnel les fait paraître intelligentes. C'est un meilleur message que d'admettre qu'elles ont trop embauché pendant la pandémie lorsque le capital était abondant en raison des faibles taux d'intérêt et d'un plan de relance financier massif du gouvernement. Pour être clair, je reconnais que l'IA fait changer le travail de nombreuses personnes. C'est difficile. C'est stressant. (Et pour certains, cela peut être amusant.) J'ai de l'empathie pour tous ceux qui sont concernés. En même temps, c'est très différent de prédire un effondrement du marché du travail. Les sociétés sont capables de se raconter des histoires pendant des années qui ont peu de fondement dans la réalité et conduisent à de mauvaises décisions à l'échelle de la société. Par exemple, les craintes concernant la sécurité des centrales nucléaires ont conduit à un sous-investissement dans l'énergie nucléaire. Les craintes de la "bombe démographique" dans les années 1960 ont conduit les pays à mettre en œuvre des politiques sévères pour réduire leur population. Et les inquiétudes concernant le régime alimentaire gras ont conduit les gouvernements à promouvoir des régimes riches en sucre, malsains, pendant des décennies. Maintenant que les médias grand public sont ouvertement sceptiques quant à la "jobpocalypse", j'espère que ces histoires commenceront à perdre de leur force (tout comme les craintes de l'extinction humaine provoquée par l'IA). Contrairement aux prédictions d'une "jobpocalypse" de l'IA, je prédis le contraire : il y aura une "jobapalooza" de l'IA ! L'IA créera beaucoup plus de bons emplois d'ingénierie IA, et je suis également optimiste quant à l'avenir du marché du travail dans son ensemble. Ce que les ingénieurs IA feront sera différent de l'ingénierie logicielle traditionnelle, et nombre de ces emplois seront dans des entreprises autres que les employeurs traditionnels de développeurs. Dans les rôles non-IA également, les compétences nécessaires changeront à cause de l'IA. Cela fait de ce moment un bon moment pour encourager plus de gens à devenir compétents en IA, et à s'assurer qu'ils sont prêts pour les emplois différents mais abondants de l'avenir ! [Texte original dans The Batch newsletter.]
idees.text_original: There will be no AI jobpocalypse. The story that AI will lead to massive unemployment is stoking unnecessary fear. AI — like any other technology — does affect jobs, but telling overblown stories of large-scale unemployment is irresponsible and damaging. Let’s put a stop to it. I’ve expressed skepticism about the jobpocalypse in previous posts. I’m glad to see that the popular press is now pushing back on this narrative. The image below features some recent headlines. Software engineering is the sector most affected by AI tools, as coding agents race ahead. Yet hiring of software engineers remains strong! So while there are examples of AI taking away jobs, the trends strongly suggest the net job creation is vastly greater than the job destruction — just like earlier waves of technology. Further, despite all the exciting progress in AI, the U.S. unemployment rate remains a healthy 4.3%. Why is the AI jobpocalypse narrative so popular? For one thing, frontier AI labs have a strong incentive to tell stories that make AI technology sound more powerful. At their most extreme, they promote science-fiction scenarios of AI “taking over” and causing human extinction. If a technology can replace many employees, surely that technology must be very valuable! Also, a lot of SaaS software companies charge around $100-$1000 per user/year. But if an AI company can replace an employee who makes $100,000 — or make them 50% more productive — then charging even $10,000 starts to look reasonable. By anchoring not to typical SaaS prices but to salaries of employees, AI companies can charge a lot more. Additionally, businesses have a strong incentive to talk about layoffs as if they were caused by AI. After all, talking about how they’re using AI to be far more productive with fewer staff makes them look smart. This is a better message than admitting they overhired during the pandemic when capital was abundant due to low interest rates and a massive government financial stimulus. To be clear, I recognize that AI is causing a lot of people’s work to change. This is hard. This is stressful. (And to some, it can be fun.) I empathize with everyone affected. At the same time, this is very different from predicting a collapse of the job market. Societies are capable of telling themselves stories for years that have little basis in reality and lead to poor society-wide decision making. For example, fears over nuclear plant safety led to under-investment in nuclear power. Fears of the “population bomb” in the 1960s led countries to implement harsh policies to reduce their populations. And worries about dietary fat led governments to promote unhealthy high-sugar diets for decades. Now that mainstream media is openly skeptical about the jobpocalypse, I hope these stories will start to lose their teeth (much like fears of AI-driven human extinction have). Contrary to the predictions of an AI jobpocalypse, I predict the opposite: There will be an AI jobapalooza! AI will lead to a lot more good AI engineering jobs, and I’m also optimistic about the future of the overall job market. What AI engineers do will be different from traditional software engineering, and many of these jobs will be in businesses other than traditional large employers of developers. In non-AI roles, too, the skills needed will change because of AI. That makes this a good time to encourage more people to become proficient in AI, and make sure they’re ready for the different but plentiful jobs of the future! [Original text in The Batch newsletter.]

La même entreprise qui a investi 13 milliards de dollars dans OpenAI et construit l'infrastructure Azure alimentant la plupart des calculs d'Anthropic vient d'examiner la facture d'un outil de codage concurrent et a décidé que cela ne valait pas la peine de payer. My Take The AI subsidy era is ending in real time. The same company that put $13 billion into OpenAI and built the Azure infrastructure powering most of Anthropic's compute just looked at the bill from a competitor's coding tool and decided it was not worth paying. That is not a productivity failure on Anthropic's end. Token-based pricing is forcing every enterprise customer to confront the actual cost of running these models at scale, and the number turns out to be far higher than the flat-rate experiments suggested. This ties directly to my Gemini Flash post yesterday. Anthropic, OpenAI, and Google all raised effective prices in the last six months. Enterprises that built workflows assuming AI costs would keep falling are now watching annual budgets evaporate in months. Two outcomes look likely from here. Either enterprises scale back AI usage to fit budgets, which slows the revenue ramp the labs need to justify their valuations ahead of IPOs, or the labs cut prices and absorb the losses, which makes the unit economics worse at exactly the wrong moment. outils.text_fr: C'est un moment vraiment spécial pour être en vie… quelques réflexions après l'entraînement de ce modèle. Aujourd'hui, nous partageons une percée sur le problème de la distance unitaire planaire, une célèbre question ouverte posée pour la première fois par Paul Erdős en 1946. Pendant près de 80 ans, les mathématiciens ont cru que les meilleures solutions possibles ressemblaient à des grilles carrées. Un modèle d'OpenAI a maintenant réfuté cette croyance, découvrant une toute nouvelle famille de constructions plus performantes. C'est la première fois qu'une IA résout de manière autonome un problème ouvert majeur au cœur d'un domaine des mathématiques.
outils.text_original: It’s a really special time to be alive…some thoughts from training this model 🧵 OpenAI (@OpenAI) Today, we share a breakthrough on the planar unit distance problem, a famous open question first posed by Paul Erdős in 1946. For nearly 80 years, mathematicians believed the best possible solutions looked roughly like square grids. An OpenAI model has now disproved that belief, discovering an entirely new family of constructions that performs better. This marks the first time AI has autonomously solved a prominent open problem central to a field of mathematics. Video — https://nitter.net/OpenAI/status/2057176201782075690#m
outils.decryptage: Le problème de la distance unitaire planaire est une énigme mathématique qui consiste à trouver la disposition la plus dense de points à une distance donnée.

outils.text_fr: Perplexity vient de publier en open source l'outil qu'ils utilisent en interne pour protéger leurs propres développeurs. 😨 Il s'appelle Bumblebee. Il fonctionne discrètement sur l'ordinateur portable d'un développeur et vérifie tout code sournois, plugins de navigateur suspects, ou outils IA qui pourraient fuiter silencieusement l'accès à vos données. Il couvre Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, tout cela. Voici pourquoi c'est important maintenant. Au cours des six derniers mois, les pirates ont discrètement glissé du code malveillant dans les blocs de construction gratuits sur lesquels presque toutes les applications du monde sont construites. Lorsqu'un développeur installe l'une de ces pièces empoisonnées, l'attaquant obtient une porte dérobée vers tout ce que ce développeur touche. Y compris ses outils IA et les clés qui les déverrouillent. La plupart des outils de sécurité défendent le produit fini. Bumblebee défend la personne qui le construit. Un chercheur indépendant en sécurité a lu tout le code et a confirmé qu'il est propre. Pas de suivi caché. Pas de collecte de données. Pas de portes dérobées. Pendant deux ans, les outils de codage IA ont été expédiés sans aucune défense de sécurité autour d'eux. Perplexity vient d'en publier un. Gratuit. Vaut la peine de l'installer si vous construisez quoi que ce soit avec l'IA.
outils.text_original: Perplexity just open-sourced the tool they use internally to keep their own developers safe. 😨 It's called Bumblebee. It runs quietly on a developer's laptop and checks for any sneaky code, suspicious browser plugins, or AI tools that might be silently leaking access to your data. It covers Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, all of it. Here is why this matters now. For the last six months, hackers have been quietly slipping malicious code into the free building blocks that almost every app in the world is built on. When a developer installs one of these poisoned pieces, the attacker gets a backdoor into everything that developer touches. Including their AI tools and the keys that unlock them. Most security tools defend the finished product. Bumblebee defends the person building it. An independent security researcher read through the entire code and confirmed it is clean. No hidden tracking. No data collection. No backdoors. For two years, AI coding tools shipped with zero security defenses around them. Perplexity just shipped one. Free. Worth installing if you build anything with AI. Perplexity (@perplexity_ai) Today we're open-sourcing Bumblebee, a read-only scanner for macOS and Linux. It checks developer machines for risky packages, extensions, and AI tool configs. Connected to Computer, it can trigger deeper scans whenever a new supply-chain risk emerges. github.com/perplexityai/bumb… — https://nitter.net/perplexity_ai/status/2057869990536360334#m
outils.decryptage: 'Open-source' signifie que le code est public. Une 'porte dérobée' est une faille de sécurité permettant un accès non autorisé. 'Supply-chain risk' désigne le risque lié aux composants utilisés dans la création d'un logiciel.

outils.text_fr: Les agents IA font progresser les mathématiques au niveau de la recherche. 🚀 Je suis ravi de partager AlphaProof Nexus de @GoogleDeepMind - un cadre agentique pour la recherche de preuves formelles alimenté par Gemini. outils.text_fr: Mistral OCR 3 renvoie maintenant des scores de confiance, au niveau de la page ou du mot. Sachez exactement à quel point le modèle est sûr de ce qu'il a extrait. Disponible dès maintenant via API et à tester dans Mistral Studio.
outils.text_original: Mistral OCR 3 now returns confidence scores, at page level or word level. Know exactly how sure the model is about what it extracted. Available now via API and to test in Mistral Studio. Video
outils.decryptage: OCR (Optical Character Recognition) : reconnaissance optique de caractères, permet de lire du texte dans des images. API : Interface de Programmation d'Application, permet à différents logiciels de communiquer.

outils.text_fr: Découvrez Stable Audio 3.0, la famille de modèles open-weight conçue pour l'expérimentation artistique. C'est notre invitation ouverte à expérimenter avec l'audio génératif. Nous pensons que les meilleures innovations sont encore à construire. Les détails sur la 3.0 : 📣 Vous possédez vos sorties, et pouvez les distribuer et les commercialiser sous la licence Communautaire Stability AI (jusqu'à 1 million $ de revenus). 🎵 Les nouvelles capacités améliorées incluent la génération de longueur variable jusqu'à six minutes, et la composition complète de chansons sur des appareils portables, sans GPU requis. ✅ Entraîné sur un jeu de données entièrement sous licence. 🎨 Vous pouvez personnaliser les modèles sur votre propre bibliothèque avec le support de l'entraînement LoRa, que nous avons documenté pour la première fois. Plus sur les modèles 👇 Vidéo
outils.text_original: Meet Stable Audio 3.0, the open-weight model family built for artistic experimentation. This is our open invitation to experiment with generative audio. We believe the best innovations are still waiting to be built. The 4-1-1 on 3.0: 📣 You own your outputs, and can distribute and commercialize them under the Stability AI Community License (up to $1 million in revenue). 🎵 New and improved capabilities include variable-length generation up to six minutes, and full song composition on portable devices, no GPU required. ✅ Trained on a fully licensed dataset. 🎨 You can customize the models on your own library with support for LoRa training, which we’ve documented for the first time. More on the models 👇 Video
outils.decryptage: Open-weight : modèle dont les poids sont disponibles publiquement. LoRa : technique d'entraînement pour personnaliser les modèles IA.
